ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Investigation into the Death of IAS Official 
*81. DR. M.N. DAS: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the investigation into the death of a senior IAS Officer, 
M.C. Mohapatra, which took place in Delhi under  mysterious circumstances 
nearly two years ago, led to any conclusive result; 
(b) if so, what are the findings; and 
(c) if not, how long the investigation is likely to continue? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) to 
(c) The matter is still under investigation by the CBI. The inquiry is expected 
to be finalized soon. 
DR. M.N. DAS: Sir, with due respect to the hon. Home Minister, Shri 
L.K. Advaniji, I feel constrained to say that a senior IAS officer, belonging to 
the Andhra Pradesh cadre, and transferred to Delhi as Joint Secrtary, died 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2000] 
under mysterious circumstances in the month of September, 1997. As of now, 
two years and six months have passed and still investigations are going on. 
Does it imply that our top intelliegence agencies work at a snail's speed, or, at 
the speed of a tortoise and not a rabbit's. If an officer of the rank of Joint 
Secretary who leaves home saying "I am going to deal with a sensitive file" 
and that too on a Holiday, i.e. Sunday and shall be back by afternoon after 
finishing the work but does not return, what can you assume? He comes out 
of his car asks the driver to bring the lunch packet and the file, enters the lift 
and within two minutes, when the attendant comes, he finds that the officer is 
not in his room. The corridor is empty, but there is some confusing noise 
outside the street. He rushes towards the end of the corridor only to find his 
master lying dead, smashed, in a pool of blood. There was a consistent demand 
that the matter be han ded over to the CBI. The officer died on 27th of 
September, 1997. The police investigated for two months; thereafter, it was 
handed over to the CBI in November, 1999. Sir, from November, 1997 to 
November, 1998—full one year —and from November, 1998 to Novem ber, 
1999 nothing happened. Another three months have gone by. If full two years 
and four months have passed and the investigation is still going on what 
impression does one get of this Government? Does it imply that the 
Government does riot mean what it s ays? Therefore, Sir, I humbly say that so 
many incidents are taking place in India, whether it is a case of an individual's 
death under mysterious circumstances; whether it is hijacking; whether it is 
massacre, whatever it is, but our intelligence machiner y has completely failed 
in dealing with such sensitive issues. I would like to know how long the 
Government will take to come to a conclusion and I would also seek an 
assurance that the investigation would be completed at the earliest. 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: Mr . Chairman, Sir, I appreciate the anguish 
expressed by the hon. Member in respect of the death of a senior official and 
the pace at which the investigations have been going on. In this particular 
case Shri Mahapatra died after falling from the upper storey of Shastri Bhawan. 
The issue is whether it is a case of suicide or homicide or accident. All attempts 
to find out these things could not be conclusive. Taking into account the 
manner in which the body was found a dummy experiment was made in order 
to see as to what would be the difference if a person is pushed and if a person 
voluntarily jumps down. A board of doctors was set up not once but twice. 
But the discrepancies persisted and no clear conclusion could be brought about. 
Therefore, it has become necessary to discuss it once again. The CBI 
2 

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
has told me that they will have to discuss this case once again with the experts 
and the doctors in order to arrive at some conclusion. I have been assured, the 
Government has been assured by the CBI that they would be able to complete 
all that can be done within a month or so. 
DR. M.N. DAS: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the public perception or the public 
suspicion is that this theory of suicide is given simply to suppress some facts 
which may be more dangerous facts. Now if somebody has to commit suicide, 
why would he come to his office and jump from a corridor on to the street. 
Supposing, he does not die. Suicide is committed after a through consideration 
that the death must be sure and certain. One would not take the risk by jumping 
from the upper floor. Supposing he fractures his body and does not die. If he 
wanted to commit suicide, he could have easily done it in his bedroom at the 
dead of night by hanging himself. But why should we come to su ch a theory 
unless conclusively established that it was a case of suicide? Let the CBI 
confess that they could not discover any clue so far as the death of this officer 
is concerned. We will be satified. The public will be satisfied. 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: Sir,  what has already been said amounts to say 
that we have not been able to come to any definite conclusion. I do not want 
to go into the arguments at this moment of time. As to what are the greater 
probabilities and whether the greater probabilities are of accident or of suicide 
or of homicide, these are matters about which it would not be proper for me 
to comment at this stage. All I can say is that the Government has been 
pursing the matter and the CBI has assured us that they will be able to give 
the final report within a month or so. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: As I understand from the reply of the 
hon. Minister, he would be in a position to know the final conclusion of the 
CBI in a month or so. My question in this connection is a little different. 
What I find is even nowadays the normal, ordinary crimes like murders and 
this type of cases are also referred to the CBI. As we understand, the CBI is 
under tremendous pressure these days. Starting from courts to Various other 
organizations, they are directly asking the CBI to take up certain matters. The 
State police and the State CID do not have that kind of confidence in the 
normal investigating agencies. Therefore, from the public perception also 
CBI's services are drawn more and more. In this context, I would lik e to 
know from the Home Minister instead of passing on every case to the CBI 
which is a specialized agency and which was created to deal with highly 
sensitive cases and not to investigate normal, ordinary crimes, whether he 
will 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2000] 
strengthen the normal, ordinary investigating agencies with the Police 
Adminstration, especially, in Delhi where the Home Ministry is directly 
involved. 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: Sir, I cannot agree more with what the hon. 
Member has said that as things stand today, there is a general tendency that in 
respect of any crime which the police is not able to solve, immediately there 
is pressure —there are requests which then, convert into pressure—that it 
must be referred to CBI. And the result is that in certain cas es where it is 
conceded, the CBI becomes overloaded With all kinds of cases. Therefore, 
there is a need to strengthen the police force. Also, in a recent Conference of 
the D.G.s of Police from all over the country and the CBI, this particular 
aspect was stressed upon. And it would be the Government's effort to move in 
this direction.

SHRI GURUDAS DAS GUPTA: Sir, part (a) of my supplementary is 
this. I understand that  the investigation is inconclusive. But will the hon. 
Minister be pleased to inform the House the following: What was the job 
which that particular officer was doing? Was he handling any sensitive case? 
And is there any circumstantial suggestion or evidenc e that it was done by 
the people who might have been alarmed because of the way in which he was 
functioning as a Government officer? Part (b) of my supplementary is this. 
Since the question of CBI has been raised, I would like to know whether the 
hon. Minister is aware that CBI has not only been overburdened, but it is also 
seriously handicapped because of the absence of a law. The CBI is functioning 
according to a Delhi Police Enactment. There is no law which empowers the 
CBI, which gives the CBI, an indep endent status, to act as an independent 
investigating agency. Therefore, considering this, and considering the need 
of strengthening the CBI, will the hon. Minister take into consideration the 
need for having a proper enactment to give CBI independence as an 
investigating agency so that it can discharge its responsibility more properly 
and independently? 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: Sir, the death of Shri M.C. Mohapatra, Joint 
Secretary in the Ministry of Mines, has been the central point of this question. 
In the cour se of the investigation, it has come on record that, at the relevant 
time, namely, when his death occurred, Shri Mohapatra was dealing with a 
file relating to the allotment of Sukanda mines, and he was feeling very 
depressed. Considerable time was taken in verifying the information in this 
regard and whatever help could be taken from the members of the family, has 
been taken. But it has not been possible to come to any firm conclusion that 
this was the reason why he committed suicide or he would have commit ted 
suicide. I can even say from what little I have gathered that the notings on the 
file in respect of Sukanda mines have been above board, have been correct. 
There is nothing wrong found in what he has done. At least, till now, it is not 
certain whether he was under pressure of any kind. But as I said in the 
beginning, the issue has been whether it is an accident or whether it is a 
homicide or whether it is a suicide. On this, some kind of conclusion may be 
arrived at after the second board completes its work and discussion is held 
with the experts and the doctors. Sir, he also asked about the law as it exists 
today and whether it handicaps the CBI. Sir, two observations have been 
made by the Supreme Court in the context of vigilance in the country, in the  
context of the CVC. The Government is pursuing that.

WELCOME TO PARLIAMENTARY DELEGATION FROM RUSSIA 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I have an announcement to make. 
We have with us, seated in the special box, members of a Parliamentary 
delegation from Russia, currently on a visit to our country under the 
distinguished leadership of His Excellency Mr. Gennady N. Seleznev, 
Chairman of the State Duma of the Russian Federation. 
On behalf of the members of the House and on my own beha lf, I take 
pleasure in extending a hearty welcome to the Leader and other members of 
the Delegation and wish our distinguished guests an enjoyable and fruitful 
stay in our country. We hope that during their stay here they would be able to 
see and learn mor e about our Parliamentary system, our country and our 
people, and that their visit to this country will further strengthen the friendly 
bonds that exist between India and Russia. Though them we convey our 
greetings and best wishes to the Parliament and the friendly people of Russia.

*83. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA' Will the Minister of MINES 
AND MINERALS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the latest estimates on industrial production for mining has 
registered nil growth during 1998-99; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the steps initiated for attaining the estimated rate in this year; and 
(d) what is the projected growth rate in this regard for the year 1999-
2000? 
12 

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES AND 
MINERALS (DR. SHRIMATI RITA VERMA): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per the estimate of the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) for 
December 1999, the growth of the mining sector was ( —) 1.7% for 1998- 99, 
and nil for the period April 1999—December 1999.  
(b) The negative growth during 1998 -99 was mainly due to fall in 
production of fuel minerals i.e. coal, lignite, petroleum (crude) and minerals 
like chromite, copper ore, gold, iron ore, manganese ore, limestone, magnesite 
and mica. The reasons for shortfall in production for petroleum (crude) were 
decline in production fr om matured fields, geological surprise, unsuspected 
increase in water cut in Bombay High reservoir and continued environmental 
problem in eastern region. The reasons for shortfall in production of coal/ 
lignite were less off -take of coal by major consumers  like power and cement 
sectors, and the reasons for shortfall in production of metallic and non-metallic 
minerals were operational constraints like break down of mining machinery, 
suspension of operation in mines, breakdown of power, as well as low demand 
for some minerals like chromite, iron ore, magnesite and manganese ore, 
limestone and mica. 
(c) and (d) Production of minerals are determined by the prevailing 
market scenario and consequently, it may not be possible to lay down definite 
targets of production for non fuel minerals. However, the Government has 
taken long term measures for development of the mines and mineral sector. 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993 for the non fuel sector was framed. The 
Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957 w as amended in 
1994 and recently in December, 1999 in order to make the mining sector 
more investor friendly and progressive. The recent amendments have 
introduced the stage of reconnaissance operations in line with global practice, 
delegated more powers to the State Governments for grant, renewal and transfer 
of mining leases for cutting down procedural delay, empowered the States to 
prevent and take action against illegal mining etc.

Harassment of Innocent people while dealing with Militants 
*84. SHRI SHARIEF -UD-DIN SHARIQ: Will the Minister of 
DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps have been taken to stop the crossing of LoC by the 
militants in J&K and the result thereof; 
(b) whether different security agencies have g iven different number of 
militants present in the State; 
(c) what is the actual number who have crossed the LoC after Kargil 
incident; 
(d) whether there is any direction to the security forces, that while dealing 
with militants, innocent citizens should not be harassed; and 
(e) if so, the reasons for which the reports of harassment of innocent 
people are coming regularly? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Appropriate measures continue to be taken against infiltration by 
terrorists. Following are some of such measures:—  
(a) T1K: army has been deployed in direct eyeball to eyeball attack with 
adversary's iroops. 
(b) All routes of ingress and infiltration are guarded any patrolled by 
our troops. 
(c) Adequate defensive and counter -infiltration postures have been 
adopted in dynamic tiers. 
(d) Retaliatory fire is brought down upon the Pakistani troops in the 
event of unprovoked firing by Pakistan, that is often taken recourse to, to 
provide cover to infiltration attempts.

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2000] 
(e) Continuous operations in the hinterland are carried out by the security 
forces to neutralise the terrorists who have infiltrated into Jammu & Kashmir. 
The army foiled 79 infiltration attempts across the LoC d uring 1999. 
124 terrorists were killed during the infiltration attempts and 36 terrorists 
were apprehended. 132 weapons were recovered. 
All figures regarding infiltration by the terrorists are, for obvious reasons, 
based on estimates. Army estimates assess  that 1650 to 1950 terrorists have 
infiltrated into Jammu & Kashmir during the post Kargil period. 
The security forces are under instructions to observe due caution to 
ensure that the human rights of innocent citizens are not violated. Regular 
training is imparted to the troops to make them aware of the human rights 
issues. Aberrations are severely dealt with. 
Many reports on human rights violations by the security forces have 
been found to be false and as having emanated from the sympathisers of 
terrorists with the intention of demoralising the security forces.

News-item regarding Mid-air crash 
*85. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of DEFENCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news -item 
"Mid-air crash averted on R -Day" appearing in Hindustan Times dated 
3.2.2000; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) whether independent inquiries have been conducted into the matter 
and if so, the findings thereof and the follow -up action taken/ to be taken in 
this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) On 26th January 2000, as part of the Republic day Parade 
flypast, a formation of three TU-142 M aircraft of Navy was required to 
22 

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
follow a composite IL -76, AN -32 & Dornier aircraft formation. Both 
formations w ere to fly together with the TU aircraft formatioxn trailing 32 
seconds behind the IL -76 formation. However, as informed by Navy, due to 
constraints of maneuvering such large aircraft in formation, the Naval aircraft 
formation which took off from its launc h base in Arakonam (in Tamil Nadu), 
arrived at the orbit point of departure (over Jhajjar in Haryana) a fraction of a 
minute early. In order to offset the effect of leaving early, the TU formation 
reduced speed to the minimum acceptable limit. But this its elf was not found 
adequate and therefore the TU formation correctly gained height to create 
vertical separation between the two formations. Though the two formations 
were in close proximity of each other, both were well aware of the air situation 
and at no  stage was there a danger of a mid -air collision. Suitable assistance 
was also provided to the two formations on the Radio- Telephone (RT) by 
Flypast control to control the situation. 
Formation flypasts involve movement of a large number of aircraft in 
close proximity and is always conducted in good visibility. Rules for formation 
flypasts are well laid out. As aircraft in formation fly past though traversing a 
similar course observe height separation, the risk of accidents particularly due 
to relative speed  between them, is extremely low. To further ensure safety, 
visual contact is always maintained while keeping vertical/lateral separation. 
Measures are taken to abort the fly pas; if visual contact cannot be maintained 
or if there is likelihood of compromis e of flight safety. However, as a 
precautionary measure, the Captain of the TU -142 lead aircraft has been 
thoroughly briefed. 
Since flight safety was not compromised and adeqeate action to ensure 
safety had been taken, a full fledged inquiry was not consid ered necessary. 
However, investigations revealed that since the TU -142 formation was a 
fraction of a minute early to set out from its departure point, it had to gain 
height to create vertical separation between it and the IL -76 formation. 
Necessary fine -tuning would be donein the composition and planning of 
flypasts in future to cater for such contingencies.

Statement 
The details of various schemes for development of jute products 
Special Jute Development Fund 
The SJDF was set up in July, 1987 with a corpus of Rs. 100 Cr. for 
integrated development of jute industry and its revival. The aim of the fund 
was to provide for holistic development of the jute sector by providing financial 
support for various schemes for improving the productivity of both raw jute 
as well as jute goods, development of indigenous machinery; research and 
development for product diversification efforts etc. 
Jute Modernisation Fund 
With a view to revitalizing the Jute Industry and giving a major thrust to 
the modernization programmes, the Government of India launched a Jute 
Modernization Fund Scheme (JMFS) with an approved outlay of Rs. 150 
crores w.e.f. November, 1986 to cater to the modernization requirements  of. 
the jute Industry. All major financial institutions with IFCI as the nodal 
agency were participating in the implementation of the scheme by lending 
funds to healthy as well as weak but potentially viable jute mills undertaking 
need based modernisation  of plant and machinery. This scheme was initially 
valid upto March, 1989 and was subsequently extended upto 1991 and finally 
upto 31.03.96. 
26 

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
National Centre for Jute Diversification 
NCJD was registered as a society in Januar y, 1992, & was formally 
launched in June, 1994. The organisation was set up to give specific attention 
towards the diversification efforts in jute sector. The organisation consolidates 
R&D results of various institutions in jute and textiles to transfer th e same to 
the entrepreneurs. It also coordinates with various agencies to help the 
entrepreneur in arranging technical, financial and infrastructural support in 
order to encourage them to take up the production and marketing of jute 
diversified products. NCJD in implementing the following schemes: 
Jute Service Centres Scheme (JSC), Raw Material Banks Scheme 
(RMB), Marketing Support Scheme (MSS), Design Development Scheme 
(DDS), Jute Entrepreneurs Assistance Scheme (JEAS), and Support to NGOs 
Scheme (NGOs). 
External Market Assistance (EMA) Scheme 
The External Market Assistance (EMA) Scheme was introduced in 1988-' 
89 to encourage the manufacturers, and export of diversified jute products till 
such time that these products could establish themselves in the exp ort market. 
The EMA is operated by JMDC out of the budgetary grant provided to them 
from the cess collected on jute products. 
UNDP Aided National Jute Development Programme 
A UNDP assisted National Jute Development Programme was launched 
in 1992 under which various R&D project have been taken up for developing 
new technologies and diversification of the jute sector. Under the programme 
Government of India in conjunction with UNDP, has provided counterpart 
funds inter-alia for the development of indigenous m achinery in the 
manufacturing sector for catering to the diversified products programme, both 
in the textile related and non -textile areas and strengthen R&D efforts in 
these fields. Phase-I of the Programme has since concluded in June, 1999. A 
second Phas e as a follow up has since been launched under the Country 
Cooperation Framework (CCF -I) for undertaking new activities and 
completion of activities under phase-I. 
The total amounts sanctioned under these programmes/schemes during

Militancy in Jammu and Kashmir 
681.  SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA:                
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: SARDAR 
GURCHARAN SINGH TOHRA: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the tempo of militancy in Jammu and Kashmir has increased 
substantially in the past six months: 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what concrete measures are being adopted to curb and control  
militancy in Jammu and Kashmir? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOMEAFFAIRS 
(SHRI CH. VIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) and (b) Though there have been 
continued efforts op the part of Pak ISI and pro- Pak militant outfits to induct 
mercenaries from across the border into J and K with a view to carrying out 
terrorist activities, the information available with the Government did not 
show any significant and sustained spurt in militancy except in the months of 
Augn»t and September 1999. 
(c) With a view to tackling  the problems of terrorism in Jammu and 
Kashmir, the Government has adopted a multi -pronged approach which 
includes, inter-alia. strengthening the border management, neutralising plans 
of the militants by proactive action against them in the hinterland, ge arin up 
intelligence machinery, greater functional framework of Operations Groups 
and Intelligence Groups of the UHQ at all levels, improved technology, 
weapons and equipments for Security Forces. 
Steps are being afresh to flush out militants and curb mili tant activities 
including closer vigil on the border, establishment of more naka parties in 
depth areas to check infiltration/exfiltration, more pickets, intensive patrolling 
and extensive cordon and search operations.

Statement-I 
Guidelines for reimbursement of security related expenditure for 
insurgency affected states in the North East 
Eligiblity Criteria for the State 
The North Eastern states have been facing serious insurgency/ militancy 
for the past several years. This  has resulted in these States having to incur 
huge expenditures for maintaining peace and tranquillity. Furthermore, the 
disturbed conditions in these States have adversely affected the economic 
development of the region, which in turn made debilitating impact upon the 
1 17 

 RAJYA SAB HA [1 March, 2000] 
revenue of these States. Lack of adequate income coupled with additional 
burden due to militancy/insurgency has completed these states to come up 
with requests to the Central Government for the reimburseme nt of additional 
security related expenditure (SRI) borne by them due to the prevailing security 
situation in the North East. 
In order to evolve guidelines for security related expenditure of an 
insurgency/militancy affected State, it may be necessary to f irst identity a 
state which can be called to be insurgency/militancy affected. A State to be 
eligible for reimbursement of expenditure needs to fulfil the following critoria. 
(i) Existence and activities by one or more banned organisation/s 
(which has been declared unlawful association under the Unlawful 
Activities (Prevention) Act. 1967) in the State. 
(ii) Deployment of para -military forces in many areas of the State for 
counter-insurgency operations. 
(iii) Declaration or part of whole of the state as dist urbed area under 
the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act. 
Items eligible for Reimbursement 
2. The Items of expenditure which will be considered for reimbursement 
by the Central Govt. Would be primarily those which have a direct bearing on 
the modernisation of Police Force in the eligible States. However, keeping in 
view the existing security scenario in these States some additional Security 
Related Expenditure (SRE) of inevitable nature which has been borne by 
these States will also be considered for reimburs ement till such time as the 
State can meet additional expenditure from within their own resources. 
Accordingly, the following items of expenditure will be considered for 
reimbursement. 
(i) Expenditure incurred by the State Govts. Including transportation 
on items like purchase of new vehicles/bullet proofing of new/ 
existing vehicles, purchase of automatic/semi -automatic weapons 
along with ammunition, bullet proof jackets and other protective 
gear and procurement of latest communication equipment, both 
mobile and static, bomb detectors, explosive detectors, computors 
etc.

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA

till such time the special scheme for modernisation of police forces in North 
East is  approved subject to the limits sanctioned by this Ministry. Bullet 
proofing of vehicles will be reimbursable to the following extent:—  
Each Police Station 1 Vehicle 
Each Coy of SAP 6 vehicles 
Each Sp 3 Vehicles 
Each DC 3 Vehicles 
VIPS As per requirement. 
As regards arms and ammunition, non bullet proof vehicles, 
communication devices are concerned reimbursement will be permissible for 
any expenditure incurred for upgradation of these items till  the norms set by 
BPR&D is achieved. 
(ii) Additional expenditure incurred in connection with capital works 
on jails and detention centres attached to police stations —the 
expenditure incurred on capital works on jails shall be as per 
Central Government norms in this regard. 
(iii)  Special training provided to State Police and Prison administration 
personnel for countor insurgency purposes. The training should 
be in designated training institutes like NEPA, Jungle welfare 
school or in a CRPF Group Centre etc. 
(iv) The Central Government already reimburses expenditure upto  a 
maximum of Rs. 9 crores per Bn. for the raising of IR Bns. by the 
State  Govts, in case of the eligible  states. If the expenditure 
incurred by them on raising IR Bns exceeds Rs. 9 crores per Bn. 
then the aditional amount will also be re -imbursed under SR E

3. Besides certain inevitale items, on which expenditure has been

provisious for CPMF/Army deployment—This may include

Increase in Power Production from Hydro Sources 
719. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is scope for increasin g power production from hydro 
spurces; 
(b) whether it is a fact that production of power from hydro sources has 
been given low priority; 
(c) if so, the reasons for neglecting the environmentally the soundest 
source of production; 
(d) to what extent Government will enc ourage private sector to produce 
power from hydro sources; 
(e) has any package been formulated; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. There is a scope for 
increasing power production from the hydro sources as only 22.39% of the 
total assessed hydro potential has been developed/ under development and 
the remaining 77.61% still remains to be developed. The main reasons for the 
slow development of hydro power include (i) Shortage of Funds and longer 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2000] 
Gestation Period (ii) Rehabilitation and Resettlement Problems (iii) Dearth of 
Good Contractors (iv) Inter- State Aspects (v) Environment and Forest 
Clearance (vi) Law and Order Problems (vii) Land A cquisition Problems, and 
(viii) Geological Surprises. 
In view of the vast scope for increasing power production from hydro 
sources, Government of India has announced a Policy on Hydro Power 
Development in August 1998 which addresses to the various issues t hat have 
led to the decline of share of hydro power in the last three decades and suggests 
remedial measures required to accelerate it. 
(d to (f) The Policy on Hydro Power Development seeks to encourage 
greater participation by private entrepreneurs and to  create the financial 
administrative and legal environment to encourage massive investment. Steps 
are also being taken to accelerate the process of survey and investigation of 
the new hydroelectric sites with a view to create a shelf of projects which 
could be taken up for execution. 
In order to encourage greater private investment, tariff for hydel projects 
has been rationalised, procedure for transfer of technoeconomic clearance 
have been simplified, a mechanism to cover geological risks has been evolved 
and State Governments have been made responsible for land acquisition, 
rehabilitation and resettlement.

720. SHRIMATI JAYAPRADA NAHATA: 
SHRI AMAR SINGH:

announced a Policy on Hydro Power Development in August, 1998 with an 
146 

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
objective to accelerate the share of hydro power which has been continuously 
declining over the last three decades. As against an ideal hydel -thermal mix 
of 40:60, the share has gone down from 44% in 1970 to 25% in 1999. Due to 
this, the peaking deficits are high, thermal stations have to increasingly back 
down as they operate under base load condition and the grid works under 
stress. The policy has, therefor, laid emphasis on timely completion of the on -

Changes in the Electricity Acts 
729. SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have recieved suggestion from Confederation 
of Indian Industries for changes in the Electricity Acts for making private 
investment more attractive; and 
(b) if so, whether government are going to consider the said suggestion? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir. Confederation of Indian 
Industry (CII) has made suggestions on changes in the Electricity (Supply) 
Act, 1948. 
(b) The Ministry of Power had a sked the National Council of Applied 
Economic Research (NCAER) as a consultant, to suggest legislative changes 
if considered necessary to accelerate the reform process. The suggestions 
made by CII were referred to the NCAER. 
The NCAER has submitted a draft Electricity Bill to replace the existing 
three electricity laws (The Indian Electricity Act, 1910. The Electricity 
(Supply) Act, 1948 and The Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998). 
The draft Bill suggests corporatisation of all the State Electricity Boards and 
their restructuring into separate entities that would provide for accountability 
based on profit centres, whether public or private; and setting up of reinforcing 
the Regulatory Commissions on the lines of the Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions Act, 1998. It stresses the need for efficiency and competitions 
with the objective of providing reliable power supply to all consumers at 
competitive prices. It also provides for a clear delineation of roles and 
responsibilities. 
In order to generate a national debate on the issue and to evolve a 
consensus on the draft Bill suggested by NCAER, its copies have been 
circulated to all concerned for their comments, suggestions and advice.

DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the total number of projects undertaken by Rajiv Gandhi 
Drinking Water Mission Authority;

togetherwith details; 
(c*) whether the State Governments were asked to set -up State level

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Rajiv Gandhi National 
Drinking Water Mission in the Department of Drinking Water Supply, Ministry 
of Rural Development, does not undertake implementation of any project/ 
scheme under Rural Water Supply Programme. 
Drinking Water Supply is a state subject. The State Governments 
implement the programme under the State Sector Minimum Needs Programme 
(MNP). The Central Government through Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking 
Water Mission supplements the efforts of the States by providing funds under 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). Powers have been 
delegated to the States to plan, sanction and implement their individual rural 
water supply schemes.

affected areas have also been delegated to the States w.e.f. 1-4-1998. However,

sanctioned by the Central Government, out of which 56 belong to Andhra 
Pradesh. 
The Government of India has introduced reforms in the Rural Water 
Supply sector with a view to institutionalise community participation in the 
rural water supply related activities. 58 districts  in various States have been 
identified for implementing the reforms on a pilot basis, out of which 4 districts 
belong to Andhra Pradesh. The project reports in respect of these districts 
have been received.

SHRI V. KISHORE CHANDRA S. DEO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir. 1 
have given a notice of privilege against the Superintendent of Police of 
Kollam District in Kerala. Sir, the hon. Member, Shri Vayalar Ravi, was 
arrested and it took one week for the police authorities to inform you. 
According to Rule 22, the Chairman should have been immediately informed. 
It took one week for the communication to originate from there. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: 1 agree with you. We will certainly look into it. 
SHRI VAYALAR RAVI (Kerala): Sir, I do not want to make any 
elaborate statement, but it was a very sad incident because we two Members 
of Parliament -- myself and Shri Ramesh Chennitala of the other House had 
been arrested at about 7.30 p.m. There was a brutal and cruel attack on my 
party office and an MLA was beaten  up. That is a different matter. We asked 
where the Superintendent of Police was. Only a junior officer was there. We 
said that we wanted to see the Superintendent of Police and talk to him. He 
refused to come, in spite of the fact that the MLA and we, Mem bers of 
Parliament, specially said that he had to come as we wanted to talk to him. 
They were evading answers. At last it was 12.30 a.m., when my wife brought 
a bedsheet and I started sleeping in the Police Station. At about 1.15, the 
Superintendent of Pol ice came. Later, we were produced before the 
Magistrate and were released in the next morning. It is very unbecoming of a 
Superintendent of Police. He was so arrogant and impertinent. He was very 
nasty in his behaviour towards the Members of Parliament. We did not have 
food. I do not want to complain about that. But, I do want to complain about 
the way the Memebrs of Parliament have been treated after arrest by a 
Superintendent of Police. We had a very bad experience of attack on the 
legislators. I believe,  Sir, this is a matter to be considered. He delayed 
informing you. I told him that he had to inform to you. I told him in the 
Police Station "now that you have arrested me, and you have come after five

which needs to be investigated.

would like to give the Government's reaction to this. We take this matter very 
seriously. Firstly, there is the form of the rule, law of co nvention requirement 
which enjoins upon the district authority that whenever any hon. Member of 
Parliament is, not simply detained, but even restrained, they are obliged to 
send the information telegraphically. That is the form of it. But the substance 
of it really goes much beyond. It is self -evident that Members of Parliament 
shall, and will, engage in political activity and their political activity could 
result in the district authorities taking recourse to certain action. But no 
matter what action the district authorities take, it is their bounden duty to treat 
every elected representative with the utmost regard and consideration. It is not

great degree of laxity in observing both the form and substance of this 
particular matter. Sir, on behalf of the Government, I urge upon you to take 
this matter most seriously and to immediately call for a full report and then 
refer this issue to the Privileges Committee because I do believe that it is 
necessary to make one or two examples so that the district authorities are 
reminded of what is an existing convention. 
After all, the hon. Member, Mr. Vayalar Ravi is a very old friend of 
mine, not very old in terms of age, but a very experienced public figure of the

we took a serious note of this

Serious situation in Assam created by ULFA 
SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN (Assam) : Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
want to draw your attention to a very serious situation which has arisen as a 
result of the killing of the P.W.D. Minister, the Forest Minister of Assam and 
three others in a bomb blast which was exploded by the ULFA on 27th 
February, 2000. This incident is related to insurgency in the region. Such 
type of killings in a hidden manner are going on in Assam which have posed 
a serious threat to the people of Assam. The unified command structure, 
comprising the Assam Police, the Central par amilitary forces and the Army, 
have failed to prevent such ghastly killings. The question that arises in the 
minds of the democratic people of our country is: "Why is such a situation 
prevailing in the State? Who is responsible for such an impasse?" 
187 

RAJYA SABHA      [1 March, 2000] 
Sir, everybody knows nowadays that Assam and the North -Eastern 
States have been badly neglected over the last fifty years. So, the anger of the 
people against the Central Government is justified. Consequently, the 
frustrated youth have become impatient and resorted to the path of 
insurgency. But to our utter surprise and dismay, the Central Government is 
quite half -hearted in tackling the problem of insurgency there. The 
Government is neither serious about negotiations with the insurgent outfits for 
finding a political solution to the problem nor have they taken proper steps to 
create a congenial atmosphere by undertaking concrete work for the 
development of the region. 
Let us take the case of negotiations. There was a possibi lity of 
negotiation with the NSCN(IM), but after the arrest of Muiva at Bangkok, the 
process was halted. Had the negotiation been taken up seriously with the 
NSCN(IM) it would have brought influence on the other insurgent outfits of 
the region. The .Government has failed to utilise this opportunity in finding a 
political solution to the problem of insurgency in Assam. 
Secondly, let me refer to the half -heartedness of the Central 
Government with regard to the concrete developmental work in the region. I 
think the latest proposals, both in the General Budget and the Railway 
Budget, with respect -to the North -Eastern region, will prove it. A very little 
has been proposed with regard to the development of this region in the latest 
Budget. Instead, there are only abstract pronouncements by the Ministers. If 
this is the ground reality, how will they be able to subside the anger of the 
people-most precisely the anger of the younger generation? How will they be 
able to bring back the frustrated youth to the right track? 
Thirdly, so far as the implementation of the Assam Accord is 
concerned, the Union Home Ministry is the nodal Ministry for this purpose. 
But the Ministry has totally failed to implement the most important aspects of 
the Accord. Firstly, the Ministry of H ome Affairs failed to detect and deport 
foreigners, as was envisaged in the Accord. Secondly, they failed to bring 
necessary changes in the statute to protect the Assamese nationality through 
constitutional, legal and administrative means, as was promised in the 
Accord. 
So, through you, Sir, I strongly urge upon the Central Government 
not to play with the anger of the people and mock at them. Instead, I urge 
upon the Government to be serious about finding a political solution to the 
188 

[1 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
problem of insurgency through negotiation and by undertaking concrete 
developmental works in the region. I also request the Central Government, 
particularly the Home Ministry, to implement the Assam Accord in letter and 
spirit. Then only, perhaps,  we may be able to come out of such an impasse 
and improve the situation in that region. Will the Central Government react 
to my suggestions?
